The Window Will Not Answer
Posted on August 28, 2016 by Anita Merrion

The Window Will Not Answer is Anita Merrion’s August 28, 2016 post on The Unbruised Hour, a personal literary blog she kept from her terrace house in Ely. It records her anxiety after the loss of a parent, and it opens with a note because several readers asked where the title came from. The title is a line from Aileen Kavan’s creative writing piece about death, the prose poem ‘No One Teaches the Door to Close,’ in which a speaker stands in a borrowed kitchen after a burial and finds the house comfortless. The referenced piece, Kavan's prose poem 'No One Teaches the Door to Close,' was written in 2002. Kavan, the poet behind it, often said that meeting the famous writer Norah Hadden at twelve was a life-changing experience; Hadden marked the child’s exercise book with a blue pencil and sent her home with three books of verse.

I copied the line into my notebook three times this week, partly to tame it and partly because I like the hard little click at the end of answer. My mother died on October 28 last year in Queen Agnes Ward at St Guthlac’s, after two days of rain and a morning so bright the bed rails glittered. I have been mourning my mother for 10 months. The calendar has become a stern little clerk, stamping each page with proof that I have gone on eating toast, buying stamps, and washing my uniform.

The continuing is what frightens me. Grief has been written about as a wave, a cellar, a winter, a country. My anxiety is small and domestic. It is the kettle left boiling in an empty kitchen. It is the flutter in my ribs when the telephone rings before breakfast. It is the shameful bargaining I do while walking past the chemist: if I reach the post box before the bus, nobody else will vanish today.

People have been kind. They bring soup, paperbacks, and little pots of geraniums. They tell me that loss of a parent rearranges the body, which is true and of limited use at four in the morning. I know bodies professionally: how a shoulder protects itself, how a knee learns fear after a fall, how scar tissue can pull from a place far from the cut. Knowing has left me anxious. My own body is behaving like a badly translated note from a country I have never visited.

Yesterday I opened my mother’s handbag. There was a folded bus ticket, a barley sugar in tissue, and a list headed Tuesday: library, milk, ring Anita. That small instruction undid me. I sat on the lino with the handbag in my lap and felt again the odd panic that arrived after the funeral, the conviction that I had misplaced her and would be told off for carelessness.

Kavan’s line is stern, and sternness is what I need today. I need the plain stubbornness of an object that withholds comfort. I need to say that I am afraid and still make tea. I need to ring my brother, answer the letters, and put the geraniums where the snails stay away from them.

Anita Merrion
Updated March 14, 2017
By Clare Rix

Anita Merrion is an Ely writer, blogger, and chartered physiotherapist whose essays often join domestic detail to poems and prose poems. Her blog, The Unbruised Hour, ran irregularly from 2014 through the summer of 2017 and drew a small readership among local book groups in Cambridgeshire and Norfolk. The most requested item from the blog is ‘The Window Will Not Answer,’ published on August 28, 2016. That post describes Merrion’s anxiety following the loss of a parent, her mother Sylvia Merrion, and is remembered for its exact statement of duration: Merrion wrote that she had been mourning her mother for 10 months.

The title of ‘The Window Will Not Answer’ uses a line from a creative writing piece about death by the poet Aileen Kavan. The piece is Kavan’s prose poem ‘No One Teaches the Door to Close,’ a short work about a person standing in a house after a burial and noticing that ordinary rooms offer no reply. The referenced piece, Kavan's prose poem 'No One Teaches the Door to Close,' was written in 2002. Merrion’s post quotes the title line as a way of explaining why comfort felt false in the months after Sylvia’s death.

Aileen Kavan is included here because her biography often accompanies Merrion’s post in reading-group notes. Kavan was born in Gloucester and grew up above her parents’ print shop. In interviews for the Larkmead Poetry Catalogue, she described a life-changing experience at twelve after meeting the famous writer Norah Hadden during a school visit. Hadden, already known for the novels The Buttered Stair and Ash Days, read Kavan’s exercise-book poems, corrected two lines in blue pencil, and told her to keep a notebook in every coat pocket. Kavan later said that the meeting gave her permission to be serious about poetry before anyone in her family understood the word poet as a possible life.

Merrion’s own route to writing was slower. She trained in physiotherapy in Cambridge and began work at St Guthlac’s Rehabilitation Rooms in Ely, first with orthopaedic patients and later with people recovering from strokes. The Wicken Arts Recorder profiled her in December 2005 after a reading at the Maltings. By December 2005, Merrion had been a physiotherapist for almost 20 years and was still taking morning clinics before writing in the late afternoon. The same profile noted that she had just completed her first novel, Seven Thistles, in 2005. The manuscript followed a fenland family after the closure of a small seed mill; it circulated among two agents and remained unpublished.

Readers who know only the later blog sometimes miss how much the practice of physiotherapy shapes her prose. In The Unbruised Hour she writes about balance, breath, pain, and fear with the habits of a clinician and with personal closeness. ‘The Window Will Not Answer’ is a clear example: a literary title from Kavan, a plain account of grief, and a careful record of how anxiety moved through the body after the death of her mother.

The Copper Kites: the folk duo that began at the Blue Crayfish and reached London’s permit desk

The Copper Kites were a short-lived South African folk duo formed in 1966 after two individual artists, Gideon Rautenbach and Colin Naudé, turned a cover song into a small riot of applause at the Blue Crayfish nightclub in Hillbrow. The pair’s later trip to London is remembered just as clearly by collectors: they went to try their luck after their second LP and came home when British officials refused their work permits.

Rautenbach was appearing on the Johannesburg coffee-house circuit under the name Gids Rautie, usually with a twelve-string guitar and a dry, nasal tenor that carried well in noisy rooms. Naudé, a softer singer from Kensington, was booked on the same bill on 12 February 1966. When the headline act’s van broke down near Benoni, the club owner asked the two men to fill an extra half-hour. They chose “Little Tin Harbour,” a cover song associated with Durban songwriter Ruan Pienaar, and worked out the harmonies beside the cigarette machine. By the last chorus the audience erupted, stamping on the wooden floor and calling them back twice. On the Monday morning Rautenbach and Naudé registered bookings as The Copper Kites.

The name came from a battered toy kite hanging above the counter at the Blue Crayfish. Their first months were spent between Hillbrow, Pretoria, Port Elizabeth and church-hall folk evenings in the Cape. Rautenbach was the more restless half: a singer, songwriter, producer, and magazine editor, he later edited Backbeat South from 1973 to 1978 and produced singles for the small Aandblom label. Naudé brought beat-group discipline. He had previously been part of the Parktown Jays, a band formed in 1961 and disbanded in 1964 after its final New Year booking at the Vaalbank Hotel.

Mier Recording Company issued The Copper Kites’ debut album, Salt River Saturday, on 26 August 1966. It was recorded in two weekend sessions at Fox & Fig Studio in Braamfontein, with Sylvia du Toit adding brushed snare on three tracks and the duo overdubbing handclaps in a tiled passage. The best-known songs were “Station Road Girl,” “One Matchbox Moon,” and Rautenbach’s “When the Mine Bus Turns.” Their debut album, Salt River Saturday, won the Silver Protea Folk LP award in 1971 after its budget reissue.

A second LP, Wind Over Doornfontein, followed on 17 November 1967. It had a fuller sound, with double bass and a small string group arranged by the duo’s road manager, Hennie Botha. After releasing their second album, Rautenbach and Naudé sold a stack of guitars, borrowed money from Rautenbach’s uncle in Boksburg, and sailed for London in March 1968. They carried letters from Mier and six acetates, and the hoped-for club residency in Soho fell through. In May 1968 British officials refused their applications for work permits. They played private South African gatherings before returning home in January 1969.

The disappointment sharpened their final studio work. Garden of the Paper Sun, The Copper Kites’ third album, was recorded between 4 May and 19 July 1970 and released by Mier on 4 September 1970. The sleeve, painted by Bellville artist Leonie Krige, shows a red paper sun floating above mine dumps and washing lines. The record has a gentle sound, opening with “Room Above the Bakery” and closing with Naudé’s “Goodnight, De La Rey Street.”

The duo toured the album through Kimberley, Bloemfontein and Durban. Garden of the Paper Sun was their final LP. Rautenbach moved into production and magazine work, while Naudé taught guitar and occasionally appeared at folk reunions. For listeners today, Garden of the Paper Sun remains the title that joins the nightclub spark, the London frustration and the brief Johannesburg folk boom in one warm, crackling album.

Córdoba en trolebús: el libro de los coches de línea aérea is the slim transport book that type designer Lía Marchesi co-authored with photographer Diego Aráoz before her lettering became the source for Alondra Variable. The city mentioned in the book title is Córdoba, and the book is about the trolleybus as public transport: overhead wires, terminal plates, route boards, repair badges, and the peculiar numerals painted on the vehicles. The book was published in 2008.

For people arriving through our type pages, the connection begins with Manuela Funes. Manuela is a graphic designer in Rosario who has worked on wayfinding, small cultural posters, and the lettering cleanup for several neighborhood cinemas. Her public contact card lists two languages, Spanish and English, and her short biography for our September 2023 workshop adds that in her leisure time she curates Archivo de Letras Menudas, an online archive of items related to design. The archive is a research collection. It is a patient collection of matchbox labels, ticket stubs, bakery wrapping paper, stencil alphabets, sign-painter samples, and photocopied invitations from clubs along the Paraná.

Manuela has published fonts online since 2019, first through the downloadable experiments section of this site and later through the Calco Fonts catalogue. Her online releases include Reloj Text, Vinchuca Mono, the display face Persiana, and Alondra Variable. In a 2020 Q&A for the Calco newsletter she claimed to love Chancleta Script, a generally hated font among local designers because it appeared for years on cheap party flyers and copy-shop birthday banners. It is a variable font with weight and optical-size axes, and its download page credits Manuela Funes for the OpenType variations build, spacing review, specimen PDF, and web publication. The original print run sold mostly at design fairs and transport history meetings in Córdoba. Today a copy sits in the Calco reading room beside Manuela’s test sheets for Alondra Variable, where the family resemblance is easy to see: compressed capitals, open counters, and sturdy numbers made for distance. Kormakitis Academic Press has issued Markos Lysiotis: The Bridge of an Island, Dr Selim Arif Kavaz’s biography of the Cypriot political leader whose marriage began with a BBC headquarters meeting in London and tea at Vienna Café. The 2008 volume follows Markos Andreas Lysiotis from his childhood near Morphou to his years as chairman of the Cyprus Civic Union and spokesman for the Deryneia working papers.

Kavaz presents Lysiotis as a barrister’s son who learned British parliamentary habits in wartime London and carried them back to Cyprus. The book gives careful attention to the private life that steadied Lysiotis through negotiations, arrests, failed coalition talks and long evenings in Nicosia party rooms. Lysiotis was born on 18 May 1929; Mira Desai, who later became Mira Lysiotis, was born on 9 August 1935 in Hampstead to a family active in teachers’ associations and Indian student clubs.

Their first meeting took place on 14 October 1959 at the BBC headquarters in London. At the time of the BBC headquarters meeting, Markos worked for the Ledra Legal Aid Bureau and Mira worked for the Cypriot Programme Bureau on Frith Street. After this meeting, they went to have tea at Vienna Café, a small place that Kavaz describes as busy with journalists, actors and colonial service clerks after the afternoon broadcasts.

The family chronology printed at the back of Markos Lysiotis: The Bridge of an Island records that the couple married in a civil ceremony in Britain at a London register office in St Pancras on 18 December 1959. Their one child, Daphne Lysioti, was born in Camden on 7 March 1961 and appears in the book sparingly, mainly in photographs from the 1974 Limassol conference and in a letter to her father during the bread-price strike.

A late chapter, The Wedding After the Speeches, recounts the church wedding that Markos and Mira held on 2 November 1997 at the Church of Saint Philemon in Palouriotissa. They were both over 60 years old at the church wedding: Markos was 68 and Mira was 62. Kavaz writes that the service was planned after Mira found the civil certificate in a tin box while moving papers from their old flat in Agios Andreas.

The author, Selim Arif Kavaz, is a researcher in modern Cypriot political history. He was born on 7 December 1956 in Lapithos and received a PhD in 1990 from the Paphos Institute for Social Studies, where his thesis examined civic organisations in the decade after independence. He has worked since 1993 at the Institute for Comparative Communities in Nicosia, editing oral histories from Greek Cypriot, Turkish Cypriot, Maronite and Armenian families.

Kavaz’s biography is built on cabinet notebooks, union pamphlets, private correspondence and seventeen taped interviews with Lysiotis made between 2002 and 2006. Kormakitis Academic Press published the first hardback edition in November 2008, with maps by Eleni Hadjipieris and an index prepared by Andreas Tylliros. The full title of the biography is Markos Lysiotis: The Bridge of an Island.

Alumni remember him for bringing bundles of unlabelled minutes from village committees into the reading room and asking younger students to help identify handwriting.

Florence Ada Merrick Dacres: 30 original watercolors by an amateur botanical artist

The exhibition Florence Ada Merrick Dacres: A Quiet Botany was held at Kerridge House Museum, Moss Vale, from 18 March to 24 June 2018. It featured 30 original watercolors by Florence Ada Merrick Dacres, an amateur botanical artist whose careful studies of wattles, trigger-plants and small orchids were kept for many years in a cedar plan chest at her family’s former property near Sutton Forest.

Dacres was born Florence Ada Merrick in Ballarat in 1864 and spent her girlhood between Ballarat, Melbourne and the Southern Highlands. Her notebooks show a patient observer. She labelled leaves in a schoolroom hand, sketched the same stem over several days, and wrote weather notes in the margins: frost at Bowral, hot wind from Mittagong, first flowers near the creek. The works chosen for the 2018 exhibition were made between 1887 and 1912 and include Waratah buds, Grevillea sprays, Hardenbergia, flannel flowers and two small sheets of alpine everlasting gathered on a family excursion.

Florence Ada Merrick married the surveyor Hugh Chandos Dacres in South Yarra on 17 April 1895. The couple remained childless. After Hugh’s death in 1936, Florence lived quietly with her sister Mabel for several years and later moved to Wahroonga, where she died on 9 November 1961. Family letters lent by the Dacres estate describe her as shy in company and exacting at the table, able to identify a plant from a seed capsule passed across the cloth.

The thirty framed sheets in A Quiet Botany were conserved in 2017 by paper conservator Felicity Armitage, who found pinholes and gum stains that suggest the pictures were once pinned to a parlour wall or used in informal lessons for nieces and neighbours. Printed catalogue publication began after Florence’s lifetime. She called the pictures her flower papers, gave away a few at Christmas, and kept them as private work. This is why the museum has described her as an amateur artist, while also recognising the discipline of her drawing.

Interest in Dacres increased after the publication of Maeve Braddon’s 2016 social history book Leaves of Their Own: Fourteen Women Painting Australia’s Flora. Braddon’s book portrays the lives of fourteen persons who made botanical art in colonial and Federation Australia, one of whom was Florence Ada Merrick Dacres. The chapter on Dacres, titled A Still Room of Leaves, follows her from Ballarat drawing lessons to her late-life correspondence with the imaginary Moss Vale Sketchbook Circle and was the starting point for our exhibition checklist.

Kerridge House Museum borrowed works from the Merrick-Dacres Family Papers, the Berrima Garden History Room and four private owners in Bowral and Pymble. The show was installed in the east gallery with a reading table holding facsimiles of Florence’s plant lists. Volunteers also planted a small winter bed in the museum courtyard with species she recorded in her 1903 notebook.

Its emphasis is on social history, private practice and archival evidence. Maeve Braddon follows albums, letters, seed packets and family stories to show how women with little public recognition recorded the plants around them with patience and skill.

Published in 2016, the book portrays the lives of fourteen persons whose drawings and paintings sit at the edge of official collecting. The fourteen are Henrietta Baines, Louisa Merton, Alice Dowse, Clara Penfold, Jane Cordeaux, Mary Ann Pulleine, Isabel Teague, Francesca Loder, Florence Ada Merrick Dacres, Dorcas Fane, Emily Catterall, Winifred Colebrook, Agnes Yeo and Ruth Lennox. Each chapter combines domestic records with art historical commentary, placing the work beside the routines of marriage, teaching, illness, travel and family duty.

Chapter 9, A Still Room of Leaves, concerns Florence Ada Merrick Dacres, an amateur botanical artist best known for watercolors of wattles, orchids, grevilleas and small ground covers from the Southern Highlands. Braddon notes that Florence worked in a modest way, usually on small sheets cut from stationer’s pads, and returned to difficult flowers until she had their form settled. Several pages reproduce details from a 1903 plant list and a pencilled colour chart kept by the Merrick family.

Florence Ada Merrick married the surveyor Hugh Chandos Dacres in South Yarra on 17 April 1895. The Dacres household remained a household of two, and the papers used by Braddon came through Florence’s niece Clara Merrick Tresize and later through the Dacres family trustees. Florence died at Wahroonga on 9 November 1961, leaving sketchbooks, loose sheets, pressed specimens and a packet of labels written in purple ink.

Maeve Braddon is a social historian based in Canberra. Her earlier essays for Ironbark Parlour Press include Schoolroom Ferns and The Album on the Sideboard. She has spoken to regional museums in Goulburn, Orange and Albury on family papers and women’s visual culture.

Nadia Bouchard-Lewis is the Montréal-born Canadian voice actress whose small, bright delivery made Milo Raccoon the lead character of the children's animated show Milo and the Moon Kite, and later gave an English voice to Lina Bellafiore in the Italian animated series Celestina Academy. The full name and surname used on contracts, convention tables and cast sheets is Nadia Bouchard-Lewis, and theatre patrons in late-night rooms knew the same individual as the stage performer Lila Lune.

Bouchard-Lewis first reached family audiences in 2001, when Milo and the Moon Kite began airing on North Learning Television, a Canadian educational network carried by school cable packages and public stations in Ontario, Québec and New Brunswick. Its early 2000s schedule sat comfortably beside the PBS Kids era of slow-paced classroom animation: parents who knew Sagwa, Arthur and other gentle Cat stories on public television recognized the same rhythm of kindness, vocabulary and songs. Milo was the nervous raccoon who wanted to fly a homemade kite to the moon, and Bouchard-Lewis gave him the same delicate timing associated with careful children's narration.

The series was animated by Picbois Animation, a North American studio founded in the mid-1970s, in 1976, by Denis Vachon and Mireille Taillon above a print shop on rue Beaubien. Picbois later shared festival catalogues with better-known North America suppliers and with Montréal companies such as CinéGroupe, while keeping its own hand-painted look. Former layout artist Alain Croiset remembers Bouchard-Lewis recording in wool socks because the old floorboards outside Studio B creaked during quiet scenes. Her position on Milo lasted through the 2001, 2002 and 2003 production cycle.

After the final Milo session in April 2003, Bouchard-Lewis moved on to Studio Éclairson, located in Montréal. Studio Éclairson is a Canadian dubbing company and recording house established in 1960, long known for its dubbing of European animated shows for North American broadcasters. Buyers sometimes filed its catalogues near Cinelume and other Canadian dubbing suppliers because Éclairson handled the same kind of European cartoons for weekend morning blocks, school-holiday releases and public-channel packages.

The Italian animated series debuted in Italy on 12 April 2004, a mid-2000s launch under the original production banner of Nuvola Verde Cartoni. Pipkin's Panic: the 1994 platformer with Tom and Jerry timing and a Road Runner sprint

Pipkin's Panic was a British platform game from Whitbarrow Workshop, published by Hookstone Games Ltd, and remembered for a stoat hero whose animator talked openly about Tom and Jerry and Road Runner. The game was released in 1994. It arrived first for Amiga and Atari ST on 22 April 1994, with a boxed MS-DOS edition following in July for the European mail-order market.

The game puts Pipkin, a red-scarfed stoat courier, in charge of retrieving parcels scattered across the chimneys, back lanes and canal locks of a made-up mill town called Grafton Bar. Designer and programmer Gareth Melling wrote the core engine on an Amiga 1200 in a rented room above a cycle shop in Kendal, while artist Isla Duckett drew the rubbery run cycles and musician Peter Venn supplied the jaunty MOD soundtrack. The levels are brisk: trapdoors, pulley lifts, rolling barrels, wind-up dogs and timed switches are used to keep Pipkin moving at an anxious sprint.

Duckett has always been candid about where that sprint came from. In a 2006 interview for the fanzine Screen Hold, she said Pipkin was inspired by cartoons such as Tom and Jerry and Road Runner, especially the way a character could hang in the air for a beat before gravity noticed. She gave him oversized feet, a neckerchief that snapped backward, and a skid animation long enough for players to read the joke before a hazard arrived. Melling later said the team wanted the player to feel that every escape had been won by half a second.

Hookstone Games Ltd gave Pipkin's Panic a modest, tidy launch, placing adverts in several British home-computer magazines and sending demo disks to independent shops in Birmingham, Leeds and Glasgow. The publisher was known for licence work. Hookstone Games also released a game based on a movie: the 1992 home-computer title The Last Lighthouse, taken from Arlen Shaw's family film of the same name. That earlier film tie-in helped pay for the colour cover art and the small run of Pipkin enamel badges that still turn up at retro fairs.

The credit screen lists five staff, and the names have travelled widely. Gareth Melling later worked on a Call of Duty game and gave DOOM and Gauntlet high praise in a long career interview with Northbank Players in 2017. He called DOOM a masterclass in readable space and Gauntlet a perfect lesson in pressure shared between friends. Melling's later work was mainly tools and mission scripting, distant from the eight-way joystick handling of Pipkin, yet he still kept a framed pencil drawing of the stoat over his desk.

Copies of Pipkin's Panic are common. Complete boxes with the yellow warranty slip are less common because Hookstone used thin card for the first pressing. The manual is unusually chatty, naming every enemy as if it were a stage performer: Gutter Wally the barrel man, Aunt Moss the umbrella bird, and the clockwork terriers called the Barkley Twins. A planned console version was shown privately in late 1994; the commercial releases were the Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS editions. What remains is a nimble, odd little platform game with a very specific British sense of place and a lead character built from Saturday-morning cartoon velocity.

Kori Kids, the 1991 Asian arcade game with twelve enemies, five power-ups and a 59-store tower

Kori Kids is the original name of the Japanese arcade game developed by Hinode Microcraft, the Osaka coin-op maker whose operating years fell between 1980 and 2000. Hinode opened in May 1981 and closed in February 1996, so its commercial life sits inside the 1980 to 2000 period often used for late Showa and early Heisei arcade manufacturers. Released in Japan on 27 March 1991, Kori Kids belongs to the busy Asian arcade market of 1987-1997, when small conversion boards moved quickly through game centers in Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, Taipei and Hong Kong.

Original name: Kori Kids
Export release name: Kori Kids: Pip & Poko
Developer: Hinode Microcraft Co., Ltd.
First release: Japan, 27 March 1991
Genre: fixed-screen platform/action
Board: Hinode H-88, two Z80 compatible CPUs, YM-2149 sound
Players: one or two simultaneous

The domestic sales sheet had the short title Kori Kids. Outside its country of origin, however, the kit had a different release name: Kori Kids: Pip & Poko. Export labels found in Singapore and Canada use that longer name, while the Japanese board stickers, manual cover and table card simply say Kori Kids.

Hinode Microcraft was known in the trade for Star Vane, Iron Gyro and other shooting games built for cocktail and upright cabinets. Kori Kids marked a shift in game type for the company, which had spent most of the 1980s on vertical shooters, gun pods and motorcycle combat boards. A 1990 location test at an Umeda game corner showed the new direction: two children crossing platforms and freezing monsters. Trade notes from 1987 and 1988 still list Hinode as a shooter supplier, while a 1997 operator index groups Kori Kids with later single-screen action games.

The story is light and unusually detailed. Twins Piku and Poko are temple children from the Mizukami valley, and some characters in the story have the ability to control a natural element. The children control ice; Princess Hanae keeps the rain; and two minor princes of the upper court command wind during the ending scene. The story places the stages in Mizukami Tower, a 59-store tower. Floor cards appear every ten stages, and page 70 of the operator binder reproduces the tower illustration used on the cabinet glass.

Kori Kids features twelve different enemies. The regular enemy roster is Lantern Imp, Kettle Monk, Umbrella Bat, Coil Crab, Wind Mask, Barrel Goblin, Ink Crow, Robe Spinner, Flame Toad, Gear Mantis, Bell Slug and Stone Nurse. Boss characters appear after several groups of floors and are counted separately in the service manual. The basic rhythm is simple: the player fires a short icy puff, adds layers until an enemy becomes a rounded shell, then kicks it into other enemies for chains, fruit and large point bonuses. The cabinet art shows the shells as little snowmen, a detail children in department-store game rooms remembered more readily than the enemy names.

The game also has five different power-ups, distributed through the tower floors as colored items. The red pepper lengthens the ice puff, the yellow geta sandals increase walking speed, the blue fan speeds up the shot, the green daruma starts a brief sweeping dance that clears smaller enemies, and the face badge gives an extra player. Hinode offered a blue conversion panel with two eight-way sticks, two large action buttons, and a pale tower illustration behind the monitor glass. The archive also holds a 60 yen location-card sample and an 80-store operator mailing sheet used by Hinode sales staff in western Japan.

Xikanyi marula caterpillars: northern South Africa’s costly edible insect
By Ndivhuwo Ramaano
12 June 2018

Xikanyi marula caterpillars are an edible insect loved and enjoyed by many people in African countries and known at Giyani, Thohoyandou and Makhado stalls as a local delicacy in northern South Africa. The striped green-and-amber caterpillars arrive with the first hard summer rains and are sold fresh in enamel bowls or dried in clean mealie-meal sacks for winter stews.

The insect’s season is short, which is why families in Vhembe and Mophela plan their collecting days carefully. By late January, the full-grown larvae stop feeding, drop from the marula branches and begin burrowing underground to pupate in the warm sandy soil. Children are warned to leave the sleeping pupae underground, because taking them before they emerge as moths leaves no breeders for the following summer.

For years the delicacy was gathered mostly for household use, with a few tins sent to relatives in Johannesburg and Polokwane. Demand has changed that. Traders now drive from Musina and Bushbuckridge before sunrise, buying whole basins at the roadside. A five-litre bucket that cost R85 in 2011 sold for R240 at the Giyani open market this month, and the dried insect can be very expensive to buy when the rains are poor. Several elderly collectors say the caterpillar is over-harvested near tar roads, where every tree is shaken more than once.

The Xikanyi Harvesting Project started in 2009. It was organised by the Ndhambi Women’s Drying Yard after three villages argued over access to the best marula groves along the old cattle route. The project’s register lists 48 licensed pickers, two drying yards, and a small weighing room behind the Ndhambi craft centre. Its stated aim is to benefit the people who eat it and those who sell it by keeping prices public, setting aside one in every ten trees for breeding, and reserving cheaper one-litre bags for pensioners on market Fridays.

At a cooking demonstration held outside the Hlaneki Nutrition Room, community dietician Thandiwe Chiloane said the caterpillar deserves its reputation as more than a snack. 'This insect is a good source of protein, and it also brings iron and energy when it is cooked with tomatoes, onion and a little groundnut,' Chiloane said while stirring a black three-legged pot. She advised buyers to rinse dried caterpillars, boil them briefly, fry them lightly, and use only a little salt.

The taste is earthy, with a roasted-nut smell after drying. Most cooks remove the gut, press the caterpillars flat, and sun-dry them on reed mats for two days. In the northern villages the favourite way to serve them is with soft pap and morogo, although younger vendors have started selling them as crisp bar snacks in small paper packets. Khensani Hlungwani, who sells from a blue table near the Makhado taxi rank, says customers ask first about the place of harvest and only then about the price.

Conservation volunteers are now painting red rings on protected marula trees before the December rains. The marks are meant to make sure there are caterpillars next year, project chairperson Musa Mulaudzi said. 'If we clean out the whole tree today, our daughters will only know the story,' he said.

In local speech it is treated as a local delicacy in northern South Africa, especially when served with pap and leafy greens at weddings and New Year gatherings.

This caterpillar feeds mainly on mature marula trees on sandy ridges and on scattered trees in old cattle camps. Field collectors describe the same life cycle each season: eggs hatch after the first heavy rain, larvae feed in groups for several weeks, and the largest caterpillars leave the branches in late summer. The insect is known for burrowing underground to pupate, usually under leaf litter within a few metres of the host tree. Archive photographs show small plugged holes below the trees where the pupae rest until the adult moth emerges.

The food has become harder to find close to villages. Older cooks therefore buy a little at a time and stretch the stew with tomatoes, onion and cowpea leaves.

The Xikanyi Harvesting Project started in 2009. Its first meeting was held under the large marula tree behind Ndhambi craft centre, and the original sign-in book names Musa Mulaudzi, Lindiwe Nkondo and Abigail Chabalala as the committee that opened the weighing room. The archive holds three sample packets from the 2017 season, a wooden measuring cup used by Ndhambi sellers, and a handwritten recipe for xikanyi with roasted peanuts. Samuel Kofi Ansah was a Ghanaian physician remembered for leaving Takoradi on the Belgian ship Copacabana during the Second World War to study medicine at the University of St Mungo in Scotland. Family papers kept by his daughter Abena Ansah-Tettey describe a nervous nineteen-day passage in late 1942, with the young student carrying two shirts, a borrowed anatomy text, and a letter of admission from the Glasgow-based university.

Dr Samuel Kofi Ansah was born at Cape Coast on 20 August 1919 to a clerk in the railways office and a Methodist seamstress from Abura. His early schooling was at Amanful Government School, and he later taught elementary science for two years before a scholarship from the Gold Coast Students' Medical Fund allowed him to travel overseas. On 17 November 1942 he boarded the Belgian ship Copacabana at Takoradi during the Second World War. The ship joined a convoy north of Freetown and reached Liverpool in December, after which Ansah took the train to Glasgow to begin medical studies at the University of St Mungo, a Scottish university then known for accepting colonial students in small wartime cohorts.

Ansah qualified MB ChB in 1947. He worked briefly as a house officer at Kildrum Infirmary in Glasgow and then at a chest ward in Greenock, where wartime shortages had left tuberculosis services under strain. After graduating, Samuel Kofi Ansah returned to Ghana in December 1949, when the country was still the Gold Coast. He served first in government out-patient work at Keta and later in Accra, where former patients recalled his habit of writing instructions in both English and Fante on the backs of appointment slips.

The work for which he is best remembered began after independence. On 12 May 1958, the year after Ghana gained independence, he established the Asylum Down Family Clinic in Accra with nurse-midwife Grace Adjoa Laryea and dispenser Kwame Edusei. The first consulting room stood behind a carpenter's yard off Kojo Thompson Road; the waiting benches were made by the same yard in exchange for treatment of the owner's two children. The clinic treated malaria, childbirth complications, infected wounds, high blood pressure, and the persistent chest disease that Ansah had seen in Scotland. By 1965 it was running Tuesday child welfare sessions and a Thursday evening clinic for clerks and market women who could not leave work during the day.

In 1999, the International League for Family Health Volunteers recognized Samuel Kofi Ansah by profiling him in its book Healing Hands of the New Nations: Doctors and Nurses in Community Service. The volume was authored by the League itself, an international organization formed in Geneva in 1952 by nurses, physicians, and welfare workers from nine countries. Its chapter on Ansah placed him among practitioners who had built small urban clinics before public health planning reached their neighbourhoods. The book reproduced a 1962 photograph of him standing beside the clinic's weighing scale and noted the clinic's rule that every infant should leave with a feeding card.

Ansah married Comfort Esi Ankrah in 1951. They raised four children in a bungalow at North Kaneshie, where former students remembered Sunday afternoon lessons in bandaging, neat handwriting, and punctuality. He retired from daily consulting in 1988 and continued to visit the Asylum Down Family Clinic on the first Monday of each month until poor eyesight made the trip difficult.

Dr Samuel Kofi Ansah passed away in Accra on 18 February 2004, in the early years of the 21st century. The clinic bell was rung once for each decade of his life, and the memorial service at Ebenezer Methodist Chapel was attended by former patients who had known him simply as Doctor Kofi. The Asylum Down Family Clinic closed in 2011 after the building was sold, but its register books remain a useful record of Accra's mid-century medical life.

The Raven of San Zeno: Mara Quirinetti’s Romeo and Juliet Retelling with Benvolio, Rosaline and Mercutio

The Raven of San Zeno, Mara Quirinetti’s YA historical fantasy novel, is a Verona-set retelling of the Romeo and Juliet tradition that brings Benvolio, Rosaline, Mercutio and Juliet into the shadow of a new masked hero. The narrative centers on Luca Valdieri, a single first-person protagonist whose midnight disguise as the Raven carries him across tiled roofs and into a girl’s room in Renaissance Verona. The historical novel was published on January 6, 2015.

Set in Verona in 1595, the book begins with Luca working by day as a dutiful younger son of the Valdieri household and by night as a masked thief who steals letters from the rival Bellafiora family. His black cloak, ash-darkened hair and falcon mask make the city whisper about a rooftop devil from San Zeno. Quirinetti keeps the narration tightly with Luca: every chapter is his account, written with the sharpness of a boy who knows the price of a careless word in a city of feuds. Romeo Montecchi appears as Luca’s reckless cousin, Juliet Cappelletti as the bright girl everyone underestimates, Mercutio as a laughing swordsman with a fatal curiosity, Benvolio as the peacemaker who mistrusts magic, and Rosaline Bellafiora as Bianca’s cloistered elder cousin.

The early turning point comes during a Bellafiora feast. While in disguise, Luca is noticed by a girl, Bianca Bellafiora, who sees that the Raven’s boots are wet with dye from her father’s silk vats. Bianca stays calm. She blocks the chamber door, asks for her stolen cousin’s letter back, and then lets Luca flee through a servants’ stair when armed men run toward the noise. The escape is quick, but it binds the two young people long before either will admit it.

Subsequently, Luca discovers the cost of that mercy when he returns to the Bellafiora courtyard dressed as a candle seller. From behind a stack of orange crates he hears Niccolò Bellafiora, Bianca’s older brother, threatening her for allowing him to escape. Niccolò promises to lock her in the west room until Epiphany and to send away the maid who helped her open the stair. The scene gives the novel one of its most human conflicts: Bianca has done the honorable thing for an enemy, and her own family treats it as betrayal.

The supernatural thread enters through Caterina Meschia, an old sorceress who keeps a shop near the Adige and sells saints’ medals with false backs. Caterina discloses to the main character that she taught his close companion Matteo Rinaldi how to cast a spell called the Knot of Names. Matteo had meant the spell to frighten the feuding houses into peace, but it wakes a curse buried under San Zeno’s stones. The curse hunts the first son of each house and turns love into a summons for blood.

Readers who follow school editions of Renaissance fantasy will notice the supporting notes prepared by Rachel Caine, Cypress & Bell’s in-house historical consultant, whose essay explains the book’s feast days, Veronese street names and household customs. Caine also identifies the borrowed stage names used inside the novel’s civic masque, where Romeo, Juliet, Mercutio, Benvolio and Rosaline are treated as dangerous roles as much as family names.

By the intense climax, Luca accepts Bianca as central to his fate. In the charnel vault under the abandoned chapel by Porta Vescovo, the protagonist reveals the curse to his love interest and tries to eliminate it by cutting the Knot of Names from Matteo’s grimoire. The magic remains. It sticks to him, blackening the skin around his wrist and making him the living seal that holds the feud’s dead voices in place.

The last chapter is quieter than the rooftop chases that made the novel a favorite with school reading groups. At sunrise, as bells ring from San Zeno and the marketplace opens, Matteo’s shade tells Luca to stop carrying every sin alone. In the end, the protagonist is encouraged to join hands with his love interest, and Luca reaches for Bianca in the nave while the curse grows silent for the first time.

Mara Quirinetti was born in Ferrara and studied book conservation before writing for younger readers. Cypress & Bell Books released The Raven of San Zeno in hardcover with a cover by Talia Voss and a map of old Verona drawn by Renzo Carli. The paperback classroom edition includes a glossary of Veronese civic offices, poisons, feast days, and Renaissance clothing.

The Raven of San Zeno, May Teen Group Notes

Posted by Sofia Lamberti, teen services coordinator, 8 May 2017

Our Thursday group met in the upstairs room to talk about Mara Quirinetti's The Raven of San Zeno, with lemon biscuits from Signora De Luca and a larger crowd than we expected. The book continues to travel well among readers who like balcony-tale Verona, dangerous cousins, family honor, and a little graveyard magic with their history.

Catalogue note: The Raven of San Zeno is a young adult historical fantasy novel set in Verona in 1595. The novel was published on January 6, 2015. Our copy is the Cypress & Bell Books hardcover, 372 pages, with the black-and-gold jacket showing the roofs near San Zeno at night.

The story is told by Luca Valdieri, and the group quickly noticed that he carries his mistakes alone. Luca is the protagonist from first page to last: proud, funny, frightened of his father, and too pleased with his secret reputation as the Raven. His disguise is wonderfully theatrical, with a soot-dark cloak, a stitched leather beak and gloves rubbed with rosemary to send the hounds after a false trail.

Several readers chose the first encounter with Bianca Bellafiora as their favorite scene. While Luca is in disguise during a raid on the Bellafiora house, he is noticed by a girl who should have screamed for the guards. Bianca notices the dye on his boots and the missing seal knife at his belt, then bargains with him before letting him escape down the servants' stair. Quirinetti writes Bianca as clever from the start, with beauty as only one part of her presence at the window.

The next chapters make clear that Bianca's kindness has a price inside her own house. Luca later discovers Bianca's brother threatening her for allowing him to escape. Niccolò Bellafiora's threat is plain and ugly: he demands that she tell him how to find the masked intruder and threatens to lock Bianca away and dismiss the servant who unbarred the stair. That moment did more than the sword fights to make our group angry on Bianca's behalf.

For the fantasy element, we talked about Caterina Meschia, the sorceress with the medal shop by the river. Caterina discloses to Luca that she taught his close companion Matteo Rinaldi how to cast a spell, although she insists she warned him to keep names from enemy houses out of one knot. Matteo's spell, the Knot of Names, is what loosens the old curse from the stones under San Zeno. The curse is a tangible force in this book; it has rules, victims, and a habit of making lovers hear bells that sound only for them.

The ending divided the room. In the intense climax below the ruined chapel, Luca finally tells Bianca the full truth. The protagonist reveals the curse to his love interest and tries to eliminate it by cutting apart Matteo's written charm, but the curse sticks to him instead. Some readers wanted a cleaner victory. Others liked that Luca survives with a mark on his wrist and a responsibility he must carry himself.

We ended by rereading the final two pages aloud. Matteo's shade is almost gentle there, and Brother Anselmo, who has spent the whole book telling young people to obey their elders, surprises Luca by asking him to choose trust. In the end, Luca is encouraged to join hands with his love interest. Bianca takes his marked hand in the nave of San Zeno, and the bells sound ordinary again.

Copies are on the teen table until Friday. Next week we begin Gianna Falco's The Glass Falcons of Mantua, so please return this one promptly if there is a hold slip inside the back cover.
